catalog.name: Antarctic Data Layers
catalog.description:
Introduction

This catalogue brings together observational products and numerical-model outputs for exploring Antarctic atmosphere, ice-sheet and solid-Earth processes, with a focus on Antarctica and the Ross Sea region. The layers include satellite-derived near-surface air temperature, coupled atmosphere–sea-ice–ocean model output, ice-sheet and glacial-isostatic-adjustment model results, and estimates of sediment thickness beneath the Ross Ice Shelf.

Data layers provided

  • Antarctic Air Temperature: daily near-surface air temperature from the AntAir ICE dataset of Bendix Nielsen et al. (2023). The source dataset covers terrestrial Antarctica, ice shelves and seasonal sea ice at 1 km grid spacing for 2003–2021. Temperature values in the source GeoTIFFs use a scale factor of 0.1, so a stored value of -300 represents -30 ℃.
  • GIA Anomaly and Global Bed Topography: outputs associated with glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), the slow deformation of the solid Earth in response to changing ice loads. These layers are model results rather than direct measurements. The global bed-topography layer name identifies the selected model run.
  • Lowry 2024 Ice Sheet Model: modelled Antarctic ice thickness for a selected simulation and time slice. Clicking the mapped layer can retrieve the modelled ice-thickness history at a location, with one line for each available model run.
  • P-SKRIPS Atmospheric Output: daily mean near-surface wind and air temperature from the Polar Scripps–KAUST Regional Integrated Prediction System. P-SKRIPS couples the Polar Weather Research and Forecasting model with the MITgcm ocean and sea-ice model for the Ross Sea region. Wind speed is calculated from the 10 m eastward and northward wind components, while the arrow layer shows wind direction and speed.
  • Ross Ice Shelf Sediment Thickness: estimated thickness of non-magnetic sedimentary cover above magnetic basement from Tankersley et al. (2022). The source study used Werner deconvolution of ROSETTA-Ice airborne magnetic observations, constrained using seismic information and Operation IceBridge magnetic data.
  • Experimental 3D Ice-Thickness Blocks: illustrative columns derived from one ice-model thickness band. Values are rounded upward into 250 m classes and positioned on the ETOPO surface; the column tops are not a reconstructed physical ice surface.

How to use the layers

Add one or more layers to the map and use the legend to interpret the displayed values. The P-SKRIPS wind arrows are designed to be overlaid on the wind-speed raster, but they can also be viewed independently. The Celsius and kelvin P-SKRIPS temperature layers show the same model field in different units. For the Lowry ice-sheet layer, click a mapped point to chart ice thickness through the available model time steps and runs.

Source datasets and methods

AntAir ICE was produced by fitting linear relationships between MODIS land or ice surface temperature and daily near-surface air temperature measured by 117 Antarctic automatic weather stations. Cloud-contaminated pixels and locations without sea ice can be recorded as no data. See the dataset and visualisation overview, Antarctic Metadata Catalogue record, published dataset and data descriptor.

P-SKRIPS version 1 is a regional coupled model developed to conserve heat and mass fluxes between its atmospheric and ocean–sea-ice components. The published experiments include summer and winter 2016 test cases over a shared approximately 10 km polar-stereographic grid covering the Ross Sea, Ross Ice Shelf and adjacent Antarctic terrain. See the dataset and visualisation overview, Antarctic Metadata Catalogue record, January case data and model paper.

Lowry ice-sheet and GIA outputs are documented in the Antarctic Metadata Catalogue. Use the run identifier and time shown in each layer name when recording or comparing results. GIA bed-topography products are available at 100-year model intervals in the source collection.

Tankersley et al. provide gridded basement elevation and sediment thickness for Ross Ice Shelf and Ross Embayment extents, including upper and lower uncertainty grids, flight-line profiles and pre-gridding basement solutions. See the Antarctic Metadata Catalogue record, published dataset, research paper and reproducible workflow. Examples of loading and analysing polar datasets are available in the PolarToolkit tutorials.

Interpretation and limitations

  1. These layers combine observations, derived products and numerical-model outputs. They should not be interpreted as having the same uncertainty or evidential status.
  2. AntAir ICE depends on cloud-free MODIS observations and statistical relationships calibrated against automatic weather stations. Accuracy varies with season, surface type, location and the number of usable satellite scenes.
  3. P-SKRIPS fields represent a particular regional model configuration and experiment. The published evaluation used one-month summer and winter test cases and was intended primarily to test coupled heat- and mass-flux conservation; it is not a general observational climatology.
  4. Ice-sheet and GIA layers depend on the selected model run, parameter choices, forcing and time slice. Compare runs before treating any one result as a preferred reconstruction.
  5. The Tankersley basement and sediment products are geophysical interpretations rather than direct maps of drilled geology. Use the accompanying uncertainty grids and source profiles for quantitative work.
  6. The experimental 3D blocks are for visual exploration only. Their vertical geometry is illustrative and must not be used as a reconstructed ice surface or as a substitute for the underlying numerical values.

Data access, licensing and citation

The AntAir ICE and Tankersley datasets are published by PANGAEA under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licences. The P-SKRIPS catalogue data are also identified as CC BY 4.0. Users should follow the citation supplied by each source repository and cite the relevant model paper when interpreting model behaviour. Licensing and citation requirements for the Lowry ice-sheet and GIA outputs should be checked in their Antarctic Metadata Catalogue record before redistribution.

Contacts

AntAir ICE: Eva Bendix Nielsen, eva.nielsen@pg.canterbury.ac.nz; Marwan Katurji, marwan.katurji@canterbury.ac.nz.

P-SKRIPS: Alena Malyarenko, alena.malyarenko@canterbury.ac.nz; Alexandra Gossart, alexandra.gossart@vuw.ac.nz.

For the Lowry and Tankersley products, use the current contact information supplied in the linked metadata records or repositories.

Disclaimer

The layers are provided for scientific exploration and informational use. They are supplied "as is" without warranty regarding accuracy, completeness or fitness for a particular purpose. Consult the original data, metadata, uncertainty information and publications before using a layer for quantitative analysis, operational decisions or safety-critical applications.

members.name: Antarctic Air Temperature 2005-07-01
members.description: Daily near-surface air temperature from AntAir ICE for 1 July 2005. Values are stored in tenths of a degree Celsius, so -300 on the legend represents -30 ℃. The legend runs from -900 to 0. Please click the parent 'Antarctic Data Layers' folder for dataset methods, limitations, access and citation details.

members.name: GIA Anomaly
members.description: Glacial isostatic adjustment anomaly in metres. GIA is the slow deformation of the solid Earth as it responds to changes in ice load. The legend uses 200 m bands from below -800 m to above 800 m. This is model output rather than a direct measurement. Please click the parent folder for source and interpretation details.

members.name: GIA Global Bed Topography
members.description: Modelled bed topography from the GIA run identified as mv1e21_fr1e24_w0p0_weakEarth_t20. Values are in metres, with the legend from -1000 m to 1000 m. Record the run identifier when exporting or comparing this layer. Please click the parent folder for source and interpretation details.

members.name: Lowry2024 Ice Sheet Model
members.description: Modelled Antarctic ice thickness at 9.5 ka (9,500 years ago) for run ism_hotf0-0_mv7-5e20_fr1e24. Values are in metres, with the legend from 0 m to 4500 m. Click a point to chart modelled ice thickness through the available time steps, with one line per model run. Please click the parent folder for source and interpretation details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Wind Speed 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean wind speed 10 m above the surface on 1 February 2017 from the displayed P-SKRIPS atmospheric output. Values are in metres per second, from 0 m/s (dark purple) to 24 m/s (yellow), and are derived from the U and V components as sqrt(u² + v²). Please click the parent folder for model methods, limitations and citation details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Wind Arrows 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean wind 10 m above the surface on 1 February 2017, shown as arrows. Each arrow points in the direction the wind is blowing and is coloured by speed in metres per second. Overlay it on the wind-speed layer or view it independently. Please click the parent folder for model methods, limitations and citation details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Atmosphere Daily Mean in Celsius 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean near-surface air temperature on 1 February 2017 from the displayed P-SKRIPS atmospheric output. Values are in degrees Celsius, with the legend from -30 ℃ to 0 ℃. This is the same field as the kelvin layer in different units. Please click the parent folder for model details.

members.name: PSKRIPS Atmosphere Daily Mean in Kelvin 2017-02-01
members.description: Daily mean near-surface air temperature on 1 February 2017 from the displayed P-SKRIPS atmospheric output. Values are in kelvin, with the legend from 243.15 K to 273.15 K. This is the same field as the Celsius layer in different units. Please click the parent folder for model details.

members.name: Tankersley Sediment Thickness 2022
members.description: Estimated thickness of non-magnetic sedimentary cover above magnetic basement beneath the Ross Ice Shelf and Ross Embayment, based on Tankersley et al. (2022). Values are in metres, with the legend from 0 m to 4500 m. This is a geophysical interpretation; consult the source uncertainty grids for quantitative use. Please click the parent folder for methods, access and citation details.

members.name: Ice thickness blocks: band 9, Ross Sea POC
members.description: Experimental 3D columns derived from ice_ds.nc thickness band 9. Thickness is rounded upward into 250 m classes and positioned on the ETOPO surface. Column height is illustrative and does not represent a reconstructed physical ice surface. Please click the parent folder for interpretation and disclaimer information.

catalog.name: Sea ice forecast
catalog.description:
Introduction

This process provides an 8-week forecast of Antarctic sea ice concentration using the graph neural network framework developed by Milz, Vetrova and Katurji (2026). Sea ice concentration is the fraction of each grid cell covered by sea ice, ranging from 0 for open water to 1 for complete ice cover. Antarctic sea ice is highly seasonal and regionally variable, and recent abrupt changes have increased the need for accurate forecasts several weeks ahead.

Forecast provided

  • Eight weekly sea ice concentration maps are available, covering forecast weeks 1 to 8.
  • The model operates on a 1-degree latitude-longitude grid around Antarctica. The legend displays concentration as a percentage, and cells below 1% are left clear.
  • A new forecast is generated each Monday, and each map is titled with the date of the forecast week.
  • Clicking a mapped location charts the forecast concentration at that grid cell across all eight weeks.

Model and input data

The forecast uses a graph neural network with an encoder-processor-decoder architecture designed to exchange information both locally and across distant but connected parts of the Antarctic domain. The research framework compared a geometric icosahedral multi-mesh with a data-driven graph built by clustering climatologically similar Antarctic regions. The model rolls the forecast forward autoregressively, one week at a time, to produce the eight forecast weeks.

Each prediction uses the preceding four weeks of ten input variables, giving 40 input channels at every grid point. The predictors are 10 m eastward and northward wind, 2 m air temperature, land-sea mask, mean sea-level pressure, sea-surface temperature, total precipitation, sea ice concentration, sea ice concentration anomaly, and sea ice concentration climatology. Atmospheric and ocean-surface predictors are derived from ECMWF ERA5, while sea ice concentration is derived from the NSIDC-0051 passive-microwave satellite product. Daily data are aggregated to non-overlapping weekly means and resampled to the common 1-degree grid.

Evaluation and key findings

The study dataset covered weekly time steps from 4 January 1989 to 9 January 2023 and was divided chronologically into training, validation and test periods. In the paper's controlled benchmark, the graph neural network achieved the lowest error on three of four sea ice concentration metrics. Its full-grid mean absolute error was about 48% lower than persistence, about 21% lower than climatology, and about 18% lower than the strongest reimplemented convolutional neural network benchmark. The graph models used roughly 4 to 24 times fewer trainable parameters than the convolutional benchmarks.

The results also show an important trade-off: the graph model generally produced the lowest average error, while IceNet achieved a lower root-mean-square error at the ice edge by about 4%, indicating fewer large local misses there. Feature-attribution analysis identified sea-surface temperature as the main source of forecast skill beyond the seasonal climatology. The paper found that graph construction mattered more than the particular message-passing operator.

How to use the forecast

Open the process below, choose a forecast week and run it to add that week's map. Compare several weeks to examine the predicted progression of the ice cover. Click a point on a forecast map to chart all eight weekly values at that location. Treat the values as model predictions rather than observations, and consult current satellite products when checking actual conditions.

Interpretation and limitations

  1. The forecast is deterministic and does not provide an ensemble range or calibrated probability, so it does not directly quantify forecast uncertainty.
  2. The 1-degree grid represents broad regional patterns and cannot resolve narrow leads, small coastal features or other fine-scale ice conditions.
  3. Forecast skill generally decreases with lead time. Errors in the recent sea ice state and meteorological inputs can propagate through the autoregressive eight-week forecast.
  4. The product forecasts sea ice concentration only. It does not predict ice thickness, ice type, floe size, drift, ridging or conditions suitable for navigation.
  5. The NSIDC pole hole is represented as zero in this visualisation and must not be interpreted as observed open water.
  6. The performance figures reported above come from retrospective research evaluation. Real-time forecasts may be affected by data latency, changing observing systems and conditions outside the historical training distribution.
  7. The paper's comparison with the operational ECMWF dynamical forecast used a smaller matched test set and interpolation from 1.5 degrees to 1 degree, so it was not a strictly like-for-like operational comparison.

Source, citation and reproducibility

The scientific source for the model is: Milz, T., Vetrova, V. and Katurji, M. (2026). Graph neural networks for Antarctic sea ice concentration forecasting. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-70984-7. The article was published online on 16 September 2026 and is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International licence.

The preprocessed research data described in the paper are available from the SICGraph data repository. Refer to the paper and repository for the complete model architecture, graph definitions, evaluation protocol and reuse conditions. The Monday update schedule and interactive map behaviour are catalogue implementation details rather than claims evaluated in the paper.

Contact

Model developer and corresponding author: Tobias Milz, School of Earth and Environment, University of Canterbury. Email: tobi.milz@canterbury.ac.nz.

Disclaimer

This forecast is provided for scientific exploration and informational use. It is supplied "as is" without warranty regarding accuracy, completeness or fitness for a particular purpose. It must not be used as the sole basis for navigation, field safety, operational planning or other safety-critical decisions.
